  • Last month's NAHB/Wells Fargo Cost of Housing Index found the median upcoming-home price is $393,300, compared to a median-priced existing home, which comes to $432,900 in the third quarter of 2026.
  • It has been revealed that builders, struggling to find buyers, are digging deeper to offer incentives on newly introduced homes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Newly introduced-construction homes are less expensive than existing ones, and the difference has never been larger, the National Association of Home Builders has found.

Last month's NAHB/Wells Fargo Cost of Housing Index found the median upcoming-home price is $393,300, compared to a median-priced existing home, which comes to $432,900 in the third quarter of 2026. That's the largest difference between new- and existing-home prices in the history of NAHB's tracking, Chairman Bill Owens noted.

It has been revealed that builders, struggling to find buyers, are digging deeper to offer incentives on newly introduced homes. The National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index plunged to a 14-year low last week. Many of the nation's major homebuilders have reported large year-over-year declines in revenue. But housing starts continue apace, showing some hope for the market long term.

“Builders are working with buyers to make latest homes more affordable and appealing in a tough market, yet the latest CHI data show housing costs still overburden families,” NAHB Chief Economist Robert Dietz said in a statement.

A typical family would have to pay 36% of their income for a median-priced existing home. They'd need 33% of their income for a upcoming home, a drop of 1% from the second quarter. And that accounts for a $17,000 drop in the median new-home price in the second quarter, when it was $434,900, NAHB found.

“As builders contend with rising construction costs, tighter lending standards and persistent labor shortages, policymakers should remove regulatory obstacles, enact permitting reform and create a stronger business environment that enables builders to produce more attainable, affordable homes,” Dietz said.

Housing costs across the board are rising. Owners are also struggling to manage insurance costs, HOA fees, and utilities.

In a recent development, NAHB's data demonstrates that the San Jose, CA, area is the most cost-burdened market in the third quarter, and 79% of a typical family's income is needed to make a mortgage payment on an existing home. Honolulu, San Diego, San Fransisco, and Barnstable Town, MA, follow. All are above 60%.

In a recent development, meanwhile, the least cost-burdened market is Decatur, IL, where 17% of a typical family's income is needed to make a mortgage payment on an existing home. Elmira, NY, Peoria, IL, Wichita Falls, TX, and Springfield, IL, all also sit under 20%.

Recent findings suggest that NAHB studied 175 markets and found that, in 95 of them, the typical family is cost-burdened, meaning they spend more than 31% of their income on a median-priced existing home. Eight of those markets are severely cost-burdened, where they pay more than 50%.

Owens said that price cuts and incentives are improving affordability. But the nation needs more pro-building laws to solve the underlying problem.

Industry observers note that "According to our latest survey, 43% cut prices in October—the highest share since 2020—and 65% offered sales incentives," Owens remarked. "But policymakers must do more to reduce red tape, address labor shortages, and fix supply chains so builders can expand the nation’s housing supply.”.

Part of the story is that it's a rough housing market all around.

Recent findings suggest that the average rate on 30-year fixed home loans jumped to 7.28% last week, up from 7.11% recorded the week before and 6.26% last year, according to Freddie Mac. Pending home sales fell to a record low in October, and existing-home sales hit their lowest level since 2010.

But part of the story is also how builders have changed up their business. The latest Realtor.com® quarterly construction insights report finds that existing homes are more expensive than newly introduced ones based on the price per square foot: $218 for new homes, $219 for existing ones.

Realtor.com senior economist Joel Berner writes that this month's new-construction data points to builders expecting tough conditions to continue.

Recent findings suggest that "Builders are dealing with a litany of obstacles to selling homes, whether it’s rising costs of land, labor, and materials, high financing costs, or weak buyer demand," Berner indicates. "This month’s data highlights them slowing down activity at the top of their funnel, which will result in slower months of starts and completions later on.".

Recent findings suggest that tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1416 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A growing body of research suggests that aging may be more flexible than once believed.
  • Industry observers note that their findings suggest that certain prescription medications and lifestyle changes can reduce biological age as measured by DNA-based blood tests.
  • The findings, published in Nature Medicine, could help scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments more effectively, although researchers emphasize that changes in biological age markers do not necessarily mean people will live longer or avoid age-related diseases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A growing body of research suggests that aging may be more flexible than once believed. Now, scientists at Yale have taken an crucial step toward identifying which treatments can actually influence biological aging and which ones show little measurable benefit.

Industry observers note that their findings suggest that certain prescription medications and lifestyle changes can reduce biological age as measured by DNA-based blood tests. Popular over-the-counter supplements examined in the research, however, showed little evidence of producing the same effects.

The findings, published in Nature Medicine, could help scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments more effectively, although researchers emphasize that changes in biological age markers do not necessarily mean people will live longer or avoid age-related diseases.

From Fighting Cancer to Understanding Aging.

When Raghav Sehgal began graduate school at Yale several years ago, he planned to use advanced computer science techniques to investigate cancer. His background in engineering and experience launching a computational biology startup had given him a strong foundation for that work.

According to recent reports, however, a question from his Ph.D. adviser at the Yale School of Medicine changed his research direction. Rather than focusing on individual diseases such as cancer or cardiovascular disease, why not investigate the aging process that contributes to their development?

"That put me on a different path," said Sehgal, now an associate research scientist in psychiatry who specializes in computational biology and bioinformatics. "As researchers, we have a long way to go in understanding the aging process and whether the steps we take to manage it really work.".

Sehgal now studies the biological mechanisms behind human aging, how scientists can measure those changes, and why getting older increases the likelihood of conditions such as cancer, diabetes, and dementia. His work also explores whether interventions might reverse certain aspects of biological aging, even if eliminating aging itself remains beyond reach.

Newly introduced DNA Tests Reveal Which Anti-Aging Treatments Work.

Sehgal is the lead author of the new study, which was conducted in the laboratory of Albert Higgins-Chen, an assistant professor of psychiatry at the Yale School of Medicine. The research team set out to determine which existing approaches to slowing aging produce changes that can be reliably measured.

Their analysis found encouraging results for certain medications and lifestyle interventions. In contrast, the over-the-counter supplements included in the study generally failed to produce meaningful reductions in biological age.

The project involved the entire Higgins-Chen laboratory, including Daniel Borrus, Jenel F. Armstrong, John Gonzalez, Jessica Kasamoto, and Yaroslav Markov.

Industry observers note that "For the first time we've shown that certain therapies have measurable impacts," noted Sehgal. "This wasn't previously possible, because we didn't have enough data to say these biomarkers are consistently responsive to these interventions.".

Biomarkers provide measurable information about what is happening inside the body. In aging research, they can help estimate a person's biological or functional age, which may differ from their chronological age.

How Scientists Measure Biological Age.

To investigate whether treatments could influence aging, the Yale team relied primarily on blood-based measurements called epigenetic clocks.

In a recent development, these tools analyze chemical patterns attached to DNA, particularly methyl groups (basic chemical structures that act like tags). Previous research has shown that these chemical markers change as people grow older. Some interventions may reverse certain age-associated patterns, and computer algorithms use those changes to estimate a person's biological age.

The researchers brought together findings from 51 clinical studies investigating different anti-aging strategies. These ranged from dietary supplements and medications to lifestyle changes and medical procedures.

According to recent reports, across those studies, the team examined more than 110 DNA methylation biomarkers (including 16 major epigenetic clocks). By comparing measurements taken before and after interventions, they could evaluate which approaches were associated with reductions in biological age.

"What we did was pretty unique," Sehgal stated. "We already know that certain things might prolong health span and lifespan. There is data from retrospective analysis as well as from animal models. We took all that knowledge along with the real-world clinical studies to identify which interventions in humans were slowing down aging across the board in these known biomarkers.".

Which Anti-Aging Treatments Showed the Best Results?

The researchers divided the interventions into four main groups: prescription drugs, lifestyle modifications, over-the-counter supplements, and medical procedures.

In a recent development, one of the clearest findings involved diet and exercise. Combining regular physical activity with a healthy eating blueprint consistently reduced epigenetic age. The dietary approaches examined included Mediterranean, low-fat, and low-carb diets.

In a recent development, the strongest reductions in biological age markers were associated with certain pharmaceutical treatments. These included metformin and semaglutide, prescription medications used to manage metabolic conditions and body weight, as well as anti-TNF therapies that target a protein involved in the body's inflammatory response.

(TNF, or tumor necrosis factor, is an immune-system protein that helps fight inflammation-related injury.).

The findings were less encouraging for over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures. In the studies examined, these approaches did not produce measurable reductions in epigenetic age.

According to recent reports, the researchers also discovered that newer biological age clocks performed better than older versions. Another important finding was that people living with diseases generally experienced larger changes in their aging biomarkers than healthy participants.

Could DNA Blood Tests Transform Anti-Aging Research?

According to Sehgal, the next priority is to test these findings in larger, more diverse populations. This would help researchers determine how consistently different treatments influence biological aging across people with different health conditions and backgrounds.

The improved blood tests could also dramatically shorten the time needed to evaluate potential anti-aging therapies.

It has been revealed that "If these new biomarkers are eventually validated to predict long-term health, scientists will be able to evaluate anti-aging therapies much faster," he added. "Instead of waiting decades for evidence from clinical trials, we'll be able to see which interventions are effective and in which people in a few years or even months.".

According to recent reports, that possibility could represent a major advance for aging research. Instead of relying entirely on clinical studies that follow participants for decades, scientists might eventually use validated biological age measurements to identify promising treatments much earlier.

However, senior author Higgins-Chen stressed that scientists must be careful about interpreting what changes in aging biomarkers actually mean.

"We have developed a rigorous, systematic approach to evaluating and comparing how biomarkers change across a wide variety of interventions, and that is a critical step in the right direction," he remarked. "However, the true meaning of that change must be fully understood.".

Crucial Questions About Slowing Aging Remain.

Although the results are promising, several major questions remain unanswered.

For example, researchers still need to establish whether changes in biological age are directly caused by a treatment or influenced by other factors that were not accounted for. They also need to understand how promptly those changes occur, whether they persist after treatment ends, and which biological processes produce them.

Most importantly, scientists have not yet established whether lowering epigenetic age leads to meaningful improvements in long-term health.

"And most importantly - what does the change mean for our long-term risk of age-related disease and functional decline?" Higgins-Chen said.

Further investigations into these questions are underway, with additional studies led by Borrus, Armstrong, and Grace Zou.

The Higgins-Chen laboratory is also affiliated with Yale's Department of Pathology, the Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Program, and the Y-Age Yale Center for Research on Aging.

What Appears to Work Against Biological Aging?

Based on the improved DNA-based blood tests, the Yale researchers identified two particularly promising approaches for reducing biological age markers:.

The analysis also identified benefits from certain anti-TNF medications, while the tested over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures demonstrated little measurable effect.

These results provide a clearer picture of which interventions may influence biological aging. However, more research is needed to confirm the findings and determine whether reductions in biological age markers ultimately translate into fewer age-related diseases, better health, or longer lives.
